questions.question: Explain why slavery was abolished in the British Empire.
questions.expected_answer: The abolitionist movement in Britain (Wilberforce, Clarkson, Sharp, Quakers, evangelicals, formerly enslaved Africans such as Equiano, women's boycotts and petitions) argued slavery was cruel and un-Christian; resistance and rebellions by enslaved people (Haiti 1791-1804, Barbados 1816, Demerara 1823, Jamaica 1831-32, Cape 1808) showed slavery was unstable and costly; economic arguments that free wage labour was more efficient (Adam Smith), declining importance of Caribbean sugar; 1832 Reform Act. Slave trade abolished 1807; Slavery Abolition Act 1833 (from 1834).

questions.question: Describe the steps towards abolition at the Cape.
questions.expected_answer: 1807-1808: end of slave imports; 1816: slave registration; 1820s amelioration laws (1823, 1826) - limits on hours and punishments, food and clothing, marriage, keeping families together, property, buying freedom, church attendance; Guardian/Protector of Slaves and punishment record books; owners protested (1831). 1 December 1834: Abolition Act in force, about 39 000 freed but apprenticed to former owners until 1 December 1838.

questions.question: What were the consequences of abolition for slave owners and freed people?
questions.expected_answer: Owners: compensated from a 20 million pound fund (Cape about 1.2 million) - less than claimed, collected in London, often sold at discount; some bankrupt; anger contributed to the Great Trek alongside Ordinance 50 and frontier insecurity. Freed people: no compensation; apprenticeship disappointing; celebrations on 1 December 1838; many left farms for towns and mission stations (Genadendal, Elim, Mamre, Pniel); but no land or money, low wages, Masters and Servants Ordinance (1841) criminalised breaking contracts, tot system; part of the community later classified Coloured; lasting inequality.
